title: C# OOP & SOLID — be precise, not encyclopaedic
exp: OOP questions at 4 YOE are not "define polymorphism." They're "show me you understand virtual/override vs new, and give me a real SOLID example from your own code."
pts: **Abstract class:** can have state (fields), constructors, and partial implementation. Use when sharing code within a related class family
**Interface:** pure contract. C# 8+ allows default method implementations, but no instance fields. Use for capabilities across unrelated types
**`virtual`/`override`:** true polymorphism — even accessed via a base reference, the derived method is called (runtime dispatch via vtable)
**`new` (hiding):** derived method only called if accessed via derived-type reference. Via base reference → base method runs (compile-time)
**SOLID:** for each principle, have ONE concrete example from your work (evidence pipeline = Open/Closed; injectable providers = Dependency Inversion)

qa.q: What is the difference between virtual/override and new (method hiding) in C#?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** virtual/override uses runtime polymorphism — C# looks up the actual runtime type and calls the override, even through a base-class reference. new (hiding) is compile-time — calling through a base reference invokes the base method, not the derived one. Hiding breaks Liskov Substitution and is usually a design smell.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: When would you choose abstract class over interface?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use abstract class when: you need to share state (fields) or concrete implementation, you need a constructor, or subclasses are closely related and share a common identity. Use interface when multiple unrelated types need the same capability, or when implementing multiple "contracts" (C# doesn't support multiple abstract class inheritance).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Operating When would you choose abstract class over interface? at scale requires understanding the runtime lifecycle, memory allocations, and underlying execution constraints. The underlying framework or storage engine optimizes execution when contracts are explicitly preserved.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Un-handled edge cases in When would you choose abstract class over interface? under high concurrent traffic can lead to performance degradation, unhandled exceptions, or unexpected memory growth. Always enforce defensive validation and error handling.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Choosing this implementation approach balances developer velocity and system performance. Senior engineers evaluate latency, operational overhead, and maintenance costs before committing.

qa.q: Give a real Open/Closed Principle example from your work.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** In ComplySec360's evidence pipeline: the core orchestration engine is closed for modification. Adding a new integration means creating a new IEvidenceProvider implementation — not editing the engine. The SCIM provisioning system follows the same pattern: each IdP is a separate IProvisioningStrategy without touching the provisioning core.
